The Big Sleep. Raymond Chandler's 1939 debut novel introduces Philip Marlowe, a Los Angeles private detective hired by an ailing millionaire to retrieve damaging photographs. The case spirals into murder, blackmail, and seduction across Los Angeles's underbelly, establishing Chandler's style of intricate plots, moral complexity, and the world-weary detective who navigates corruption with dry wit.

Philip Marlowe is hired by the aging General Sternwood to recover compromising photographs related to a blackmail scheme. The case quickly branches into multiple murders, missing persons, and a pornography ring, each thread tangled with the others. Marlowe moves through the criminal underworld of Los Angeles—gamblers, hustlers, crooked cops, and dangerous women—with sardonic charm.

He becomes entangled with Sternwood's daughter Carmen, who is unstable and dangerous, and her sister Vivian, who hires him and seduces him. The investigation reveals that the original photographs and blackmail are tied to a powerful pornographer and arms dealer. Marlowe must navigate double-crosses and lies from everyone around him, including the police.

The novel culminates in a confrontation that clarifies the murders and motivations, though ambiguity remains about Sternwood's own complicity. Chandler pioneered the sophisticated hard-boiled detective novel with this work, creating the template for the thinking man's private eye operating with moral code in an amoral city. Los Angeles's underbelly becomes as developed as any character in the story.
